intuition: Read the string one position at a time. For a letter, try its lowercase and uppercase forms. For a digit, keep it unchanged. Continue each choice through the remaining positions, then save the completed string. Each sequence of letter-case choices gives one result.

Build the result left to right using a character path. For a letter, recurse once with its lowercase form and once with its uppercase form. For a digit, recurse once with the unchanged character. Taking one allowed variant at every position describes every possible final string exactly once.

After each recursive branch, remove its character before trying the next choice. When the path reaches the input length, join it into a fresh string. Starting with explicit lowercase and uppercase variants also handles input that is already uppercase without depending on its original case.

steps: For s=a1b2, start at index 0 with an empty path. Character a offers the two choices a and A.
Follow lowercase a first. Digit 1 has one unchanged choice, giving partial path a1.
At character b, first choose lowercase b. Digit 2 is unchanged, completing a1b2.
Backtrack to b’s decision and choose uppercase B instead, completing a1B2.
Backtrack to index 0 and choose uppercase A. The same choices at the remaining positions generate A1b2 and A1B2.
Return those four strings. Digits 1 and 2 have never branched or changed, and every letter-case combination is represented.

codeNotes.note: Letters branch into two distinct cases. The one-element digit tuple prevents duplicate branches for characters with no case variation.
Joining only at a completed path creates an independent result string and avoids repeatedly rebuilding prefixes during recursion.
Undo exactly the character chosen by this branch so its sibling starts with the same prefix rather than accumulated choices.

keyDecision: Only letters branch into two choices. Digits have one unchanged choice.

concept.question: Why do digits continue one path while letters split it in two?
intuition: Enumerating all character replacements would change digits and introduce invalid strings. Only alphabetic positions have two permitted choices; digits remain fixed.

concept.observation: Only letters branch; every character retains its original position.
approach: Advance through the input positions in order.
Choose both cases for each letter and one unchanged choice for a digit.
Record each completed text and undo choices to explore the other paths.
concept.correctness: Every branch changes only the current letter to one of its two allowed cases or preserves the current digit. A complete path is therefore valid. Every legal case assignment chooses exactly one branch at each letter, so the search includes all possibilities without duplication.

complexity.explanation: There are two-to-the-letter-count outputs, each requiring the full text length to write. The working prefix and recursion depth are linear in text length, besides the exponential output.

pitfalls: Only letters branch; every character retains its original position.
